caption: Send this to someone who doesn’t know who decides what our children learn in school #education #drmartinlutherkingjr #malcolmx #politics #news
audio_track_actual: A masked narrator's voiceover interleaved with archival audio clips of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. No music bed; word-tracking subtitle overlays.
video_overlay_text_observed: A masked presenter (silver face mask, white headdress, suit) seated at a desk; opening subtitle 'THE PERSON WHO'. Highlighted single-word subtitles track the narration throughout.
audio_content_summary: Argues that 'who decides what your children learn' is the real story behind why MLK is canonized in U.S. schools while Malcolm X is comparatively sidelined. Splices a real MLK clip calling Israel 'one of the great outposts of democracy in the world' against Malcolm X's defense of Palestinians and his on-camera answer to being called anti-Semitic ('how can I be anti-Semitic when the Arabs are Semitic'). Claims MLK's speechwriter was Jewish and 'wrote I Have a Dream,' while Malcolm X was sympathetic to the Palestinian cause — and that this explains the curricular asymmetry and MLK's national holiday. Closes on Robert Maxwell: Ghislaine Maxwell's father and an alleged Mossad agent who bought Macmillan and 'used it to control the contents of the textbooks distributed to American school children… rewriting our past.'
implied_frame: Mixed. Group A (verified, carded at 1988-maxwell-macmillan-001): Maxwell did complete a ~$2.5–2.6B takeover of Macmillan, a major U.S. education publisher, in 1988. The MLK and Malcolm X quotes are also real — MLK called Israel 'one of the great outposts of democracy' in a March 25, 1968 address to the Rabbinical Assembly; Malcolm X criticized Zionism in 'Zionist Logic' (1964) and gave the cited anti-Semitism answer on camera. Group C (unsupported): the causal spine. Both King and Malcolm X are standard figures in U.S. curricula; MLK's federal holiday (signed 1983, first observed 1986) reflects his role as the movement's central figure, not a documented decision to bury Malcolm X over Israel. The 'Jewish speechwriter wrote I Have a Dream' line conflates two different people — Stanley Levison, King's Jewish advisor who edited speeches, and Clarence B. Jones, the African-American attorney who drafted portions of the 1963 March on Washington address (the 'I have a dream' passage was largely improvised). And Maxwell's ownership of Macmillan is documented; his alleged editorial control of textbook content to 'rewrite the past' is not.
